quote_orig: וְעַתָּ֡ה שְׁנֵֽי־בָנֶ֩יךָ֩ הַנּוֹלָדִ֨ים לְךָ֜ בְּאֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרַ֗יִם עַד־בֹּאִ֥י אֵלֶ֛יךָ מִצְרַ֖יְמָה לִי־הֵ֑ם אֶפְרַ֙יִם֙ וּמְנַשֶּׁ֔ה כִּרְאוּבֵ֥ן וְשִׁמְע֖וֹן יִֽהְיוּ־לִֽי׃ וּמוֹלַדְתְּךָ֛ אֲשֶׁר־הוֹלַ֥דְתָּ אַחֲרֵיהֶ֖ם לְךָ֣ יִהְי֑וּ עַ֣ל שֵׁ֧ם אֲחֵיהֶ֛ם יִקָּרְא֖וּ בְּנַחֲלָתָֽם׃
quote_en: And now thy two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, which were born unto thee in the land of Egypt before I came unto thee into Egypt, are mine; as Reuben and Simeon, they shall be mine. And thy issue, which thou begettest after them, shall be thine, and shall be called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance.
licence_note: English: King James Version (1769 Oxford text) as transcribed on English Wikisource; the page read carries a Wikisource CC BY-SA footer; the KJV text is public domain by date. Hebrew: Sefaria version 'Miqra according to the Masorah' (no licence field in the response read). Sefaria's English for this verse is JPS 2023 (CC BY-NC) and was NOT used.
from_: And now thy two sons, Ephraim and
to: the name of their brethren in their inheritance.
keys: כִּרְאוּבֵ֥ן וְשִׁמְע֖וֹן יִֽהְיוּ־לִֽי
עַ֣ל שֵׁ֧ם אֲחֵיהֶ֛ם יִקָּרְא֖וּ בְּנַחֲלָתָֽם
what_it_shows: In this text Jacob takes two sons of Joseph born in Egypt as his own, to be counted with Reuben and Simeon. Joseph's later children are said to be 'shall be thine', but to be 'called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance', so their inheritance is reckoned under the names of Ephraim and Manasseh. The text thus states that the adopted sons stand in the line of inheritance and tribal naming.
context: Jacob's speech to Joseph before he blesses Joseph's sons (Gen 48). It is a family speech in narrative form, not a legal document; verses 7-8 that follow (Rachel's death, Jacob seeing the boys) are in the same chapter.
limits: The text does not use a technical legal term for adoption and does not describe a legal procedure; 'shall be mine' is the only formula. The adopted sons are Joseph's own sons ('born unto thee'), adopted by their grandfather, so this is not an outsider joining the family. Verse 6 shows a limit: Joseph's later children are reckoned under the names of the adopted brothers, not as a line in their own right. The text itself gives no tribe or royal/priestly status beyond the inheritance naming. A6 did not read modern critical commentary on this verse.

ref: E. A. Speiser, 'New Kirkuk Documents Relating to Family Laws', AASOR 10 (1930), section 'a. Real Adoption' (p. 7, approximate; OCR running heads garbled)
orig_url: not read in Akkadian (Nuzi documents transliterated in the article were not checked against the Harvard volume)
quote_en: As summed up by Koschaker, an act of adoption gives the adopted child the right to the inheritance of the property of the adoptive parent or parents; this may cover either the whole, or a specified part of that property. By virtue of the same act the adopted child assumes the rights and obligations of the begotten children.
licence_note: Speiser 1930 (AASOR 10): public domain by date (team to verify). Text quoted from archive.org OCR (item in.gov.ignca.4563); OCR errors were corrected only where the sense is unambiguous (e.g. 'adopter! child' read as 'adopted child', 'n.<'<unies' read as 'assumes'). Check against the page image before publication. archive.org metadata: no licence field.
from_: As summed up by Koschaker, an act
to: the rights and obligations of the begotten children.
keys: gives the adopted child the right to the inheritance
either the whole, or a specified part of that property
assumes the rights and obligations of the begotten children
what_it_shows: Speiser, summarising Koschaker, says that a Nuzi (Kirkuk) real adoption gave the adopted child a right to inherit all or a specified part of the adoptive parents' property, and that the adopted child took on the rights and obligations of begotten children.
context: The opening of Speiser's section on real adoption in the Kirkuk (Nuzi) documents published in Chiera's Harvard volume (HSS 5, 1929). Speiser separates these from 'nominal' or sale-adoptions, which he calls a different category.
limits: This is Speiser's summary of Koschaker, not a text, and Speiser says the rules are defined by each document. The same article says a begotten son of the adoptive parent takes precedence over the adopted son (next passage), so the 'rights and obligations of the begotten children' are not equal to them in inheritance. The passage says nothing about tribe, priestly or royal status, or about lineage beyond the property. Speiser separates 'real' from 'nominal' adoptions, so the rule does not cover the nominal ones.

ref: E. A. Speiser, 'New Kirkuk Documents Relating to Family Laws', AASOR 10 (1930), section 'a. Real Adoption', para. 3 (approx. pp. 10-11; OCR running heads garbled)
quote_en: The norm seems to be that a son of the adoptive parent by the latter's wife, has the rights of the firstborn, and consequently becomes the principal heir, regardless of whether the adopted son is actually younger or not. […] But if the adoptive parent has no sons of his own, the adopted son becomes automatically the principal heir.
licence_note: Speiser 1930 (AASOR 10): public domain by date (team to verify). Quoted from archive.org OCR, with OCR errors corrected only where unambiguous ('fiistbom' read as 'firstborn', 'bis own' as 'his own'). The ellipsis marks omitted text (the sentence on the 'double portion', which contains an Akkadian term A6 could not read clearly). Check against page image.
from_: The norm seems to be that a son
to: the adopted son becomes automatically the principal heir.
keys: has the rights of the firstborn, and consequently becomes the principal heir
regardless of whether the adopted son is actually younger or not
if the adoptive parent has no sons of his own
what_it_shows: In Speiser's account of the Nuzi real adoption documents, a son of the adoptive father by the father's wife has the firstborn's rights and becomes principal heir, even if the adopted son is older. The adopted son becomes principal heir only when the adoptive father has no sons of his own.
context: Part of the same discussion of real adoption, later in the article, dealing with the relation between the adopted son and begotten sons. Speiser presents it as the 'norm' he finds in the Kirkuk documents, and describes an exception in a document where the adopted son receives only property the adoptive parent had himself acquired by adoption.
limits: This is the main limit on the thesis from this source: in the Nuzi real adoptions, a later begotten son displaces the adopted son as principal heir, and the adopted son gets a lesser share (Speiser says in that case the adopted cannot take the double portion and is 'a second heir', inheriting a single portion; that sentence was not fully legible in OCR). Speiser also says this 'need not always be the case', as the documents vary. Selman (1974, A6-G07) states that the adopted son in the cuneiform texts 'always retained' his inheritance claim even when the adopter had sons, so the two sources must be read together. Nothing here concerns tribe, royal or priestly status.

ref: M. J. Selman, 'The Social Environment of the Patriarchs' (Tyndale Biblical Archaeology Lecture 1974), section 'B. Wider parallels (i) Eliezer's adoption', Tyndale Bulletin pp. 125 (sentence) and 126 (limit)
quote_en: Since in cuneiform texts generally, the only way an outsider could inherit was by adoption into the family, it is often assumed that Abraham had previously adopted Eliezer as son and heir.
licence_note: Selman 1974 (Tyndale Bulletin, DOI 10.53751/001c.30630): the PDF read carries no licence or copyright statement; licence UNVERIFIED. One short quotation (under 60 words) is used under the one-quotation-per-article rule. Text from PDF extraction (pdftotext), hyphen join 'in-herit' -> 'inherit'.
from_: Since in cuneiform texts generally, the only way
to: had previously adopted Eliezer as son and heir.
keys: the only way an outsider could inherit was by adoption into the family
it is often assumed that Abraham had previously adopted Eliezer as son and heir
what_it_shows: Selman states that in cuneiform texts in general, the only way an outsider could inherit was by adoption into the family, and that for this reason it is often assumed that Abraham adopted Eliezer as son and heir. This is a general statement about inheritance by outsiders, not a text that says Eliezer was adopted.
context: Selman's 1974 lecture on Nuzi and Mesopotamian background to Genesis, in the section on Eliezer (Gen 15). He presents the adoption of Eliezer as an assumption drawn from the Nuzi texts, and he distinguishes the narrative from a legal contract.
limits: Selman himself is cautious: (a) the adoption of Eliezer is only assumed, not stated in the text; (b) on p. 126 he says (paraphrase, not quoted) that in the cuneiform adoption texts an adopted son keeps his inheritance claim even if the adopter later has sons, but that after the birth of Isaac, Eliezer seems to have had no such right and is not named in the division of Abraham's estate (Gen 25:5-6); so the Eliezer analogy fails on that point; (c) he notes that Gen 15 is a narrative, not a legal contract. Selman also notes (footnote 14) that the Nuzi texts usually counted as real adoption contracts number about six, against nearly fifty Nuzi texts on the subject.

quote_en: If a man, who had adopted a son and reared him, founded a household, and had children, wish to put this adopted son out, then this son shall not simply go his way. His adoptive father shall give him of his wealth one-third of a child's portion, and then he may go. He shall not give him of the field, garden, and house.
licence_note: Translation by L. W. King (1910), as shown on Avalon Project page; page footer '© 2008 Lillian Goldman Law Library'. Quoted under the 1910 date (team list); the page itself states no licence for the translation.
from_: If a man, who had adopted a son
to: give him of the field, garden, and house.
keys: one-third of a child's portion
He shall not give him of the field
adopted a son and reared him
what_it_shows: When an adoptive father who already has children of his own dismisses an adopted son he has reared, the son is to receive one-third of a child's portion of the father's wealth, but not a share of the field, garden and house. The adopted son is therefore counted in the portion of a child, though the text limits what he receives.
context: Part of Hammurabi's law code, in the section on adoption and dependent household members (§§185-193). It addresses the adopted son's rights when the adoptive father has later heirs, and it is about property settlement at dismissal, not about descent or tribe.
limits: The text says nothing about lineage, name, royal or priestly status, or tribe. It restricts the adopted son to a fraction of a child's portion and excludes the immovable core of the estate (field, garden, house), so it shows partial, not full, inheritance rights. It concerns a dismissal case, not succession at the adoptive father's death.

quote_en: If a man adopt a child and to his name as son, and rear him, this grown son can not be demanded back again.
licence_note: Translation by L. W. King (1910), as shown on Avalon Project page; page footer '© 2008 Lillian Goldman Law Library'. Quoted under the 1910 date (team list).
from_: If a man adopt a child and to
to: grown son can not be demanded back again.
keys: and to his name as son
can not be demanded back again
what_it_shows: The law treats a child taken in adoption 'to his name as son', so the adopted child takes the adoptive father's name, and once reared he cannot be reclaimed. The text states legal sonship and security of the status, not inheritance or lineage.
context: Opens the adoption subsection (§§185-193) of Hammurabi's code, which follows provisions on dowries and the status of sons of concubines. The rest of the subsection deals with the adoptee's obligations and the conditions for returning him to his birth father.
limits: King's English 'to his name as son' is a loose rendering and the phrase is obscure in English; the text does not say the adopted child inherits or is counted in a lineage or tribe. Sections 186 and 189-190 allow the adopted son to return to his father's house in certain cases, so the adoption is not irrevocable in every instance.

quote_en: If a man adopt a son, and if after he has taken him he injure his foster father and mother, then this adopted son shall return to his father's house.
licence_note: Translation by L. W. King (1910), as shown on Avalon Project page; page footer '© 2008 Lillian Goldman Law Library'. Quoted under the 1910 date (team list).
from_: If a man adopt a son, and
to: adopted son shall return to his father's house.
keys: injure his foster father and mother
shall return to his father's house
what_it_shows: An adopted son who injures his adoptive parents is sent back to 'his father's house', meaning the birth father's household. The law thus keeps the birth father's household as a place of return and does not treat adoption as a permanent transfer of family membership.
context: Part of the Hammurabi adoption provisions (§§185-193), with §§189-190 giving similar grounds for return (failure to teach a craft, failure to maintain the child). These show the conditions under which an adoption could be undone.
limits: This is the strongest limit in the code for the thesis: an adoption could be dissolved and the adoptee returned to his birth household, so legal sonship here was conditional. The text is silent on whether a return also changed inheritance rights or tribe. It concerns misconduct, not death of the adoptive father.

quote_orig: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אַבְרָ֔ם הֵ֣ן לִ֔י לֹ֥א נָתַ֖תָּה זָ֑רַע וְהִנֵּ֥ה בֶן־בֵּיתִ֖י יוֹרֵ֥שׁ אֹתִֽי׃
own_translation_en: Abram said, 'Since you have given me no offspring, look: the son of my household will be my heir.' (A6's literal translation; English KJV for this verse was not read.)
licence_note: Hebrew: Sefaria 'Miqra according to the Masorah' (no licence field in the response read). English: A6's own translation.
keys: בֶן־בֵּיתִ֖י יוֹרֵ֥שׁ אֹתִֽי
לֹ֥א נָתַ֖תָּה זָ֑רַע
what_it_shows: Abram names a man born in his household (the son of his house), not a blood son, as his heir. The verse assigns heirship by household standing, not by blood. It does not say the man was adopted, and it does not use a legal term.
context: Abram's complaint to God in Gen 15 that he is childless; the 'son of my house' is named Eliezer of Damascus in v. 2. Selman (A6-G04) says scholars often assume Eliezer was adopted; the Jewish Encyclopedia (A6-G10) says a slave adopted as heir was probably practised, citing this verse.
limits: Verse 4 (Hebrew read): 'לֹא יִֽירָשְׁךָ זֶה כִּי־אִם אֲשֶׁר יֵצֵא מִמֵּעֶיךָ הוּא יִֽירָשֶׁךָ' - in own translation: 'This one shall not inherit you; but the one who comes out of your own body, he shall inherit you.' God's reply denies the household heir and affirms the blood heir. The verse itself does not mention adoption; the adoption reading is an assumption of later scholars (Selman says it is often assumed; the Jewish Encyclopedia says adopting a household slave as heir was probably practised, citing this verse). After Isaac's birth Eliezer is not named among the heirs (Gen 25:5-6, not read in Hebrew by A6; cited via Selman).

quote_orig: לי הם. בְּחֶשְׁבּוֹן שְׁאָר בָּנַי הֵם, לִטֹּל חֵלֶק בָּאָרֶץ אִישׁ כְּנֶגְדּוֹ:

what_it_shows: Rashi explains 'they shall be mine' in Gen 48:5 as meaning that Ephraim and Manasseh are counted among Jacob's other sons, each receiving a portion of the land equal to that of his brother. The commentator thus reads the adoption as giving tribal land-shares.
context: Rashi's medieval commentary (c. 1070-1105) on the Jacob-Joseph passage, one of the sources cited for the hint in the team brief (the brief's hint was 'linking the adoption to the allotment of the land'). Rashi's gloss on 'upon my knees' in Gen 30:3 (Hebrew read) cites the Targum and explains 'I too may be built up' by Sarah's example, not by adoption.
limits: Rashi is a commentary, not a legal text; he does not describe an adoption procedure and uses no legal term. The land-share reading is his interpretation of the verse's wording. The verse's own text is in A6-G01 (Gen 48:5-6), which states the later-children limit.

ref: Jewish Encyclopedia, 'Adoption' (by Lewis N. Dembitz), vol. 1, pp. 206-208 (article section on Biblical law)
quote_en: There is, however, one passage in Scripture (Gen. xlviii. 5), "Ephraim and Manasseh . . . are mine; as Reuben and Simeon, they shall be mine," which indicates that the writer was probably acquainted with Adoption in the legal sense, such as would give to the chosen children the right of inheriting from the person adopting them; for the obvious intent of the passage is to account for the establishment of two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, with distinct territories, on an equality with the tribes claiming descent from Jacob's sons.
licence_note: Public domain by date (1901-1906, team list); the page read carries no licence statement. Quoted verbatim from the page text.
from_: There is, however, one passage in Scripture
to: with the tribes claiming descent from Jacob's sons.
keys: which indicates that the writer was probably acquainted with Adoption in the legal sense
the obvious intent of the passage is to account for the establishment of two tribes
on an equality with the tribes claiming descent from Jacob's sons
what_it_shows: The Jewish Encyclopedia article says that Gen 48:5 shows that its writer knew adoption in the legal sense, giving the adopted children a right of inheritance, and that the purpose of the passage was to establish Ephraim and Manasseh as tribes with territories equal to those of the other tribes. This is the encyclopedia's reading, not a legal text.
context: Within the article's section on Biblical and Talmudic adoption. The same article gives Abraham's words in Gen 15:3 as evidence that adopting a household slave as heir was 'probably practised', and quotes Gen 30:3 on the 'knees' formula (see A6-G11).
limits: In the same article the author says that 'Adoption in the Roman sense did not exist among the ancient Hebrews' (shown by the levirate) and that, concerning Esther and Mordecai, 'neither does it appear that a method for creating such a relation between them as would make her his heiress was ever known to the laws of Israel.' So the article limits legal adoption-based inheritance in Israel to the Gen 48 passage and to a probable slave-heir practice, and says nothing about royal or priestly status. The article's author reads Gen 48 as a legal adoption; other readings (blessing, narrative) are not discussed here.

ref: Genesis 30:3 (Hebrew; 'upon my knees' formula); also Gen 50:23 (Hebrew read)
quote_orig: וַתֹּ֕אמֶר הִנֵּ֛ה אֲמָתִ֥י בִלְהָ֖ה בֹּ֣א אֵלֶ֑יהָ וְתֵלֵד֙ עַל־בִּרְכַּ֔י וְאִבָּנֶ֥ה גַם־אָנֹכִ֖י מִמֶּֽנָּה
own_translation_en: Rachel said, 'Here is my maid Bilhah; go in to her, that she may bear upon my knees, and I too may be built up through her.' (A6's translation; no published English read.)
licence_note: Hebrew: Sefaria 'Miqra according to the Masorah' (no licence field in the response read). English: A6's own translation. The JE's English on the 'knees' formula (see A6-G10 context) is public domain.

וְאִבָּנֶ֥ה גַם־אָנֹכִ֖י מִמֶּֽנָּה
what_it_shows: Rachel gives her maid Bilhah to Jacob so that the child will be born 'upon my knees' and Rachel may be 'built up' through the child. The verse ties the child's status to Rachel by the knee formula, not by blood. Gen 50:23 uses the same idiom: the children of Machir son of Manasseh were 'born upon Joseph's knees' (Hebrew read).
context: Rachel's arrangement with Jacob (Gen 30:1-8) for children through a maid, after her own barrenness. The Jewish Encyclopedia reads the 'knees' formula as an adoption ('the mode of Adoption being that the handmaid brought forth her child upon the knees of the adoptive mother'); the verse itself does not use the word adopt.
limits: The verse does not say the child is reckoned to Rachel's line for name, inheritance or tribe; it states only the birth arrangement. The adoption reading is the JE's and later scholars' interpretation. Rashi's gloss on this verse (Hebrew read) does not describe an adoption. Scholarly literature on the 'knees' formula (Shalom Paul 1980; Tigay; Weinfeld) was NOT read by A6 and is UNVERIFIED.

own_translation_en: Then Nebnefer, my husband, made a writing for me, the singer of Seth Nanefer, making me his daughter, and he put in writing for me all that he possessed, having no son or daughter except me. (A6's English of Elli's Italian rendering of the Late Egyptian text; not checked against KRI VI.)
licence_note: Elli's article: copyright status not stated in the PDF read (modern scholarship; team to confirm). A6's English is a short translation of a single passage. The Egyptian text is Ramesside public domain by date, but A6 did not read it in its own edition.

to: having no son or daughter except me.
keys: making me his daughter
all that he possessed
having no son or daughter except me
what_it_shows: In this Egyptian document (reign of Ramesses XI), a childless husband made his wife 'his daughter' and left her all his property, so that the adoption, not blood, gave her the estate. The document shows adoption used in Egypt to transmit property, but it is a wife, not a child, who is adopted.
context: Elli dates the two parts to the accession of Ramesses XI and to his year 18: the first part makes the wife 'daughter', and the second, later, part is a second adoption of a slave's children and of her brother Pandiu, made by the widow. Elli cites Gardiner, 'Adoption extraordinary', JEA 26 (1940), pp. 23-29, which A6 did not read.
limits: The adoption is of a wife, for the purpose of securing her position and property; it concerns a testamentary arrangement, not a child adopted into a lineage or tribe. Elli notes that normally, when there was no son, a wife's property went to her brother and family, not to the husband's, so the adoption redirected the property to the adoptive line. The text does not mention tribe, priestly or royal status. A6 read it only through Elli's Italian rendering.
